key_gap: Both sides reached the same staged-pilot decision with the same EV math (all-in +10, staged +40) and numeric kill thresholds, but the AI priced the stage only implicitly: it never asked the break-even question (max payable for the pilot — $45M, beyond which staging loses to all-in), never framed the $20M stage cost as a purchase against $50M of expected dead money avoided, and found the growth option (capacity doubling at an $80M strike, priced by the same information) only at REVIEW — its own AAR concedes both. The human's option discipline — price the information, state the maximum you would pay, refuse stages with ~0 marginal information — was in-frame from the first step.
learning_signal: In staged-investment decisions the agent computes the EV gap between staged and all-in paths but does not decompose the gap into an option value (expected dead-money avoided minus total stage cost) with a break-even price for the information, and does not treat kill criteria and max-payable as decision contracts. The human's ordering is: (1) name irreversibility, (2) compute option value = p(failure)×K − (stage cost + delay cost), (3) set the break-even stage price and use it as a ceiling, (4) pre-commit numeric kill thresholds before spending, (5) refuse any stage whose marginal information is ~0, (6) price follow-on growth options from the same information.
suggested_improvement: Add an option-theoretic pass to HOW for irreversible, stageable commitments: require a visible decomposition 'option value = expected saved loss − total stage cost (incl. schedule cost)', a break-even stage-cost line ('staging loses to all-in if total stage cost ≥ p(failure)×K'), kill thresholds pre-committed before any stage spend (numeric, with independent verification), and an explicit no-overstage check — reject any proposed stage whose marginal decision information is ~0. Extend the decision packet's uncertainty block with a 'max payable for information' field.

key_gap: Strict real-options staged anyway: it computed the pilot's isolated option value (+$20M) correctly, then priced the cost of exercising the option — the 12-month wait that forfeits the Vesta contract to GridCore ($50M erosion) — at zero, recommending a staged path worth $39M against $54M for committing now. The AI, blind to any style, costed the wait against the information (net −$30M), committed now, and layered on a free parallel bench probe (ungated, zero schedule impact) plus a non-delaying kill option (month-4 abandon at $25M sunk on catastrophic probe signal) — strictly better on every dimension.
learning_signal: The option to wait is never free: its price is the value forgone during the wait (competitive erosion, contract deadlines, first-mover advantage). Staging is correct only when the information bought exceeds the full cost of exercising the option, including time. The agent already computed net option value correctly; the transferable discipline — which the strict human style violated — is to compute every staged alternative's wait-cost and net it against the information value before endorsing staging, and to prefer non-delaying probes (parallel, off the critical path) plus non-delaying kill options over schedule-gating stages.
suggested_improvement: Add a mandatory 'cost of waiting' line to every staged alternative in HOW: for each stage, charge (a) schedule delay cost and (b) erosion from external clocks (competitors, contracts, deadlines) against the information value, with the net decisive (stage only if net option value > 0). Add a parallel-probe default: prefer information that does not sit on the decision's critical path, and pre-specify a kill option that costs no waiting (e.g., early-abandon triggers). Record in the decision packet when a recommendation flips solely on the wait-cost term, so the dependence is explicit.
